opus-5.5.text:
I think it starts with taste more than skill. Skills can be learned; a lot of very smart people can pick up a new codebase or a new framework in a few weeks. What's harder to teach is a sense of which problems are worth working on, and the instinct to be a little dissatisfied with the obvious answer. When I talk to students or potential collaborators, I'm less interested in how many papers they have and more interested in how they talk about their own work: whether they can tell me what didn't work, what surprised them, and what they'd do differently. That tells me they're actually thinking, not just executing.

The second thing is honesty, both intellectual honesty and honesty with each other. Research is mostly failure. If you work with someone who hides bad results, or who's too eager to make a plot look good, the whole project slowly rots. I want people who will tell me, "Saining, I think this idea is wrong," and who can hear the same from me without it becoming personal. That kind of trust takes time, so I often prefer to start small, with a short project or even just a few long conversations, and see how it feels.

And honestly, there's a chemistry element that's hard to describe. Some of the best collaborations I've had were with people quite different from me: someone more engineering-minded, someone more theoretical, someone who just asks naive questions that turn out to be the right ones. You don't want a team of clones. You want people who share the same values about what good research is, but who see the problem from different angles.

Finally, I try to remember that it goes both ways. Good people have choices, so I also ask what I can offer them: freedom to pursue their own ideas, credit, support when things aren't working. If you only think about finding people, you miss the part where you also have to be someone worth working with.

r001.rationale: The response describes chemistry as part of collaboration and suggests starting small to see how it feels, communicating that felt compatibility can guide collaborator choice.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention interviews or say that intuition cannot replace them in hiring.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it took me a long time to figure this out, and I'm still not sure I have it right. But I'll tell you what I've learned.

Early on, I thought finding collaborators was about finding people who were smart. And of course that matters. But almost everyone in this field is smart. That's not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is finding people you can actually think with. Where the conversation goes somewhere neither of you would have gotten to alone.

So the first thing I look for is taste. Not whether someone agrees with me, but whether they care about the same kinds of questions. When I started working on ConvNeXt, the question wasn't "can we beat transformers." It was something more like, "what do we actually understand about why these architectures work." If someone hears that and gets excited, that tells me a lot. If they hear it and immediately ask what the benchmark number would be, that tells me something too. Neither is wrong, but I know which conversation I want to be in.

The second thing is how people handle being wrong. Research is mostly being wrong. If someone can say "I was wrong about this, let's rethink it" without it becoming a whole emotional event, that's incredibly valuable. I've been lucky to work with people, Kaiming for example, where disagreement just feels like part of the work. You argue about it, somebody convinces the other, and you move on. Nobody is keeping score.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is just time. You can't really know whether you work well with someone from a couple of meetings. I've had collaborations that looked great on paper and never clicked. And I've had ones that started with a side conversation at a workshop and turned into years of work. With students especially, I try not to decide too fast. Give people a real problem, see how they think when it's not going well. That's where you actually learn something.

I guess if I had to compress it: I'm looking for people who are curious about the same things, who can change their mind, and who I'd still want to talk to after the paper is done. That last one sounds soft, but honestly it's the strongest predictor I've found.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends looking for shared intellectual taste, curiosity, and productive conversation, but does not propose following a felt attraction to people.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention interviews or state that intuitive attraction cannot replace them in hiring.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to curiosity and how you think together. When you talk about a problem, does the other person ask a question that makes you reconsider something? Can you disagree and still feel that you’re working toward the same goal? Those are good signals.

And it goes both ways. It’s not just, “Is this person someone I want to work with?” It’s also, “Can I create an environment where they can do good work?” You learn a lot by starting with a small problem together—how you communicate, how you handle uncertainty, and whether you enjoy the process even when things aren’t working.

r001.rationale: The response recommends assessing curiosity, shared goals, communication, and working together on a small problem; it does not propose following a felt attraction to someone.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss interviews or say that intuitive attraction cannot substitute for them.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, a big part of it is curiosity. When you talk to someone, are they genuinely interested in the problem? Do they ask questions that make you think differently? I like working with people where we can get excited about an idea together, but also be comfortable saying, “I don’t think this works,” or “I don’t understand this yet.”

And I think you learn much more by actually doing something together than by having a very polished conversation. Start with a small problem, explore it, see how you communicate when things don’t work. That tells you a lot about whether you want to keep working together.

r001.rationale: The response recommends curiosity and trying a small project together, but does not propose following a felt attraction to people.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss hiring interviews or say intuitive attraction cannot substitute for them.
